title: Crito
author: Plato
openingChapterLabel: Chapter I — The Visit at Dawn
openingText: SOCRATES. Why have you come at this hour, Crito? it must be quite early. CRITO. Yes, certainly. SOCRATES. What is the exact time? CRITO. The dawn is breaking. SOCRATES. I wonder that the keeper of the prison would let you in. CRITO. He knows me because I often come, Socrates; moreover, I have done him a kindness. SOCRATES. And are you only just arrived? CRITO. No, I came some time ago.
about:
Crito visits Socrates in prison at dawn, bringing a plan to help him escape. Socrates has been condemned to death, but the sentence awaits the return of the sacred ship from Delos. Crito expects the ship that day. Socrates believes it will arrive the following day, and that he will die the day after its arrival.

Crito appeals to friendship, reputation, responsibility for children and the practical possibility of escape. Socrates asks a different question: would escaping be just? He insists that one must never do wrong, even in response to wrong, and that living well matters more than simply staying alive.

In the final part, Socrates imagines the Laws of Athens speaking to him. They argue that his lifelong residence in the city commits him to its laws: he must persuade the city or obey it. The dialogue leaves readers with a difficult test of political obligation, personal integrity and loyalty to friends. This edition presents the complete dialogue in three reading sections.

angleCards.title: The argument for staying.
angleCards.text: Crito has every practical reason on his side: friends, money, escape, exile, sons left behind. Socrates listens to all of it and refuses. Trace the argument by which he does — and ask whether it would convince you in his place.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the moral argument Socrates makes for refusing escape — the contract with the laws, the duty to the city — and ask whether it holds up against the practical case Crito brings.

angleCards.title: The Laws of Athens speak.
angleCards.text: In the final part of the dialogue, Socrates imagines the Laws of Athens addressing him directly. Read the speech as both an argument and a dramatic voice.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Laws of Athens speech as a literary device — what it accomplishes, why Plato lets the city speak rather than have Socrates argue, and what the rhetorical effect tells us about the moral claim.

angleCards.title: Justice over survival.
angleCards.text: Socrates asks whether escape would be just, rather than treating survival as sufficient reason to flee. Test the strength of that principle when the judgment against him is itself unjust.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the radical claim that a person should never act unjustly, even to save their own life — and test whether Socrates's commitment to it is admirable, naive, or both.

angleCards.title: The most personal philosophy.
angleCards.text: Socrates has a chance to escape death, but asks whether the principles he has defended still bind him. Read for the tension between his argument and the personal cost of following it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how Socrates applies his principles while awaiting execution, and whether his reasons justify his choice.

cast.name: Socrates
cast.description: Condemned to death and awaiting execution in Athens. He refuses to decide whether to escape on practical grounds alone. He asks whether flight would be just and whether he can abandon principles he defended before his conviction.

cast.name: Crito
cast.description: Socrates' old friend, who visits him at dawn. He offers money and help from friends, including contacts in Thessaly, to make escape possible. He worries about Socrates' children, his friend's life and what others will think of those who failed to save him.

cast.name: The Laws of Athens
cast.description: The personified Laws speak in the argument Socrates imagines. They claim that the city has enabled his upbringing, education and family life, and that his decision to remain in Athens amounts to an agreement to obey its laws.

cast.name: The Many
cast.description: The wider public whose judgment worries Crito. Socrates distinguishes popular opinion from the judgment of someone who understands justice, using physical training as an analogy.

cast.name: The Expert
cast.description: The hypothetical figure Socrates introduces to make the case against Crito's appeal to public opinion. In matters of physical training, you listen to the trainer, not the crowd. In matters of medicine, you listen to the doctor. In matters of justice — the most important of all — you listen to the one who actually knows. The figure is mostly absent from the action of the dialogue, but the argument depends on him.

cast.name: Socrates' Children
cast.description: Crito argues that Socrates should stay alive to raise and educate his children. In the Laws' speech, Socrates addresses that concern: taking them into exile would deprive them of Athenian citizenship, while good friends should care for them whether he is in Thessaly or dead.

whyItMatters.title: Consent and Political Obligation
whyItMatters.body: The Laws argue that Socrates has accepted their authority by choosing to remain in Athens while being free to leave. This makes the dialogue a useful starting point for examining consent, citizenship and the limits of obedience. Does accepting a state's benefits mean accepting every judgment it makes?

whyItMatters.title: Justice as the Only Question
whyItMatters.body: Crito argues from every other consideration — money, friendship, family, reputation, the practical. Socrates rules them all out. The only question, he insists, is whether escape would be just. Living, dying, what people think, what one's sons need — none of these can override the question of justice. The clarity of that move is part of why Crito remains philosophically provocative. Socrates is not making a sentimental claim. He is arguing that justice is a separate kind of consideration, not commensurable with the others. Modern ethics has been arguing about whether that move is right, and what its costs are, ever since. The dialogue is a short, exact statement of one of the most extreme positions in moral philosophy.

whyItMatters.title: Practising What He Defends
whyItMatters.body: Socrates refuses to abandon an argument simply because his own life is now at stake. The dialogue asks whether consistency is enough to justify a decision, and what a commitment to justice demands when friends and family bear some of its costs.
